newsitem.title: USA: N.Y., California losing jobs; other states gain.
newsitem.headline: N.Y., California losing jobs; other states gain.

text.p: New York and California are the big losers in the battle to retain companies and jobs, while Georgia and four other South Atlantic states are among the big winners, according to a Dun & Bradstreet study released Tuesday.
The study found that more than 56,000 businesses have moved across state lines, resulting in the relocation of more than 1 million jobs between 1991 and 1995.

It ranks the 50 U.S. states; Washington, D.C.; Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands based on the net gain of employees, the difference between the number of workers entering and leaving the state due to business or job relocation, during that period.

"The real effect of business migration is much greater than the numbers you see here," said David Kresge, senior vice president and chief economist at D&B, a unit of the Dun & Bradstreet Corp., a major provider of credit and marketing information.
"Each direct job lost or gained has a multiplier effect within the local economy, affecting retailers, financial services and state tax revenues."

New York and California, ranked 53th (last) and 52nd respectively, each suffered a net loss of more than 3,000 businesses and more than 75,000 jobs in the five-year period. California suffered its greatest job loss in 1991, while New York suffered its greatest loss in 1995, D&B said.

Nearly half of the South Atlantic states (Georgia, Delaware, Virginia, Florida and Maryland) were in the top 10, with the region as a whole posting the largest net gain in businesses (3,824) and direct employment (72,544) from relocation during the five-year period.
"The cost of doing business in many South Atlantic states provides an attractive incentive, particularly when compared with the high costs of doing business in New York and California," Kresge said.

"Georgia, ranked 1st, offers low manufacturing wages and moderate taxes as incentives to attract businesses from throughout the country. Florida, ranked 9th, attracted a larger inflow of small businesses by offering moderate wages with a low tax burden. Virginia -- ranked 6th, and Maryland, ranked 10th -- also gained large inflows of jobs by capturing the outflows from Washington, D.C."

Colorado, ranked 4th, had the strongest performance of all states in the Mountain region with a net gain of 13,908 jobs, D&B said. While the South Atlantic states had their greatest surge of migration in 1991, the Mountain states have been on a steady upward trend attracting businesses.

Collectively, the Mountain states showed a net gain of 37,092 jobs over the five-year period, 58 percent of which came from California. The region offers California businesses significant cost savings in lower wages and taxes. Colorado also boasts the best-educated population outside Massachusetts and Connecticut, D&B said.
Regional differences in cost structure and labour characteristics also affected the kinds of employers that moved into a region, it added.

Nationwide, manufacturers accounted for 16 percent of all companies moving, but 31 percent of all employment. Manufacturing jobs accounted for a much higher proportion of job gains in the South Atlantic states.
In total, 750 manufacturing companies brought 55,680 jobs into the South Atlantic region during the early 1990s, 77 percent of the net employment gain from all industries, D&B said.
Manufacturing accounted for 55 percent of total employment lost from the Pacific region and 41 percent of job loss in the Mid-Atlantic states, it said.
